title: Caution needed on premium payment change
full_text:
SMSF members using their fund to pay a premium for life insurance are not restricted as to which individual’s account those monies are deducted from, but must ensure other members and future beneficiaries are not impacted by their decision, according to a sector educator.
Heffron SMSF education specialist Natasha Panagis said superannuation law allows insurance premiums to be deducted from either a member’s accumulation or pension account, subject to the governing rules of the fund, provided those expenses are allocated in a fair and reasonable manner.
“This means those premiums should be deducted from the account of the member whose life or health is being insured because that member is the one receiving the benefit of the insurance cover and any future insurance proceeds,” Panagis said during a recent presentation hosted by The Auditor’s Institute.
“Where members typically run into trouble is where premiums for one member’s insurance are deducted from another member’s account because it’s difficult to argue that’s fair and reasonable when the other member receives no corresponding benefit from the policy.
“From an audit perspective, it’s worth checking those premiums and any proceeds are allocated to the correct member accounts. It’s quite a simple issue, but one that is commonly overlooked, particularly in multi-member funds.”
She pointed out the issue of which account a premium was deducted from became even more important if the insurance beneficiaries were not the member, noting trustees also had to act in their best interest.
“Can the insured member change their mind and choose to deduct premiums from a different account balance in the future?” she said.
“They can change where the premiums are coming out, but trustees should be careful because they are under an obligation to perform their duties in the best interests of beneficiaries.
“Any change could be made at the member’s direction and properly documented, particularly where it could affect the ultimate beneficiaries, and it’s important to check that because there could be estate planning reasons why premiums were deducted from a particular account.
“For example, you could have a blended family where the accumulation account would be going to adult kids from a previous marriage and the pension account will go to the second spouse.
“If we’re changing where those insurance premiums are being deducted from, say from accumulation to pension account, when those proceeds get paid, they’re going into the pension account, which means the second spouse will receive them instead.
“The trustee really needs to look at it holistically and work out what is the right thing to do here.”
